title: Transfer: Replace Words with Their Shortest Root
oneLiner: Replace every word in a sentence by the shortest dictionary root it starts with. Same trie, but now you look for a stored word that is a prefix of the query.
keyTakeaway: Mark the node where each root ends. To shorten a word, walk its letters down the trie and stop at the first end mark: that is the shortest root. Falling off the trie first means no root fits, so keep the word. Each word costs at most its own length, however many roots there are.
explanation:
This follows Trie: Prefix Search with the question turned around. You get a dictionary of roots and a sentence of lowercase words separated by single spaces. Replace each word that starts with some root by the shortest such root, leave other words alone, and return the new sentence. With roots cat, bat and rat, "the cattle was rattled by the battery" becomes "the cat was rat by the bat".

In the parent lesson the query was the prefix, and the answer was how many stored words continue it. Here the stored roots are the prefixes, and for each query word you want the shortest stored root that it starts with. The naive way checks every root against every word: with r roots that is O(r · L) per word.

Build the trie from the roots as before, but instead of a count, mark the node where each root ends (an IsEnd flag). For a word, walk its letters from the root of the trie. After each letter, if the node you are on is marked, the letters so far are a root, and since you are walking from the shortest prefix up, it is the shortest one: stop and use it. If the next letter has no child, no root fits this word: keep it unchanged. If the word runs out before any mark, keep it too ("ab" is not shortened by the root "abc").

Building costs O(total length of the roots) and each word costs at most its own length, so the whole job is linear in the input size. Stopping at the first mark is also why a longer root such as "catt" never wins over "cat".

The visualization walks each word of "the cattle was rattled by the battery" through a trie of cat, bat and rat.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Trie: Prefix Search. In which direction does the prefix relationship go in each problem, what did you store on the nodes instead of a count, and why is the first end mark you meet the shortest root?

testCases.inputDisplay: ["cat", "bat", "rat"], "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
testCases.expectedJson: "the cat was rat by the bat"

visualizationSteps.message: Insert the roots cat, bat, rat into a trie and mark the node where each one ends. Then walk every word of the sentence.
"the": no root starts with 't', so the walk falls off at once. Keep the word.
"cattle": walk c, a, t and land on an end mark after "cat". Stop there: replace the word with "cat".
"was": no root starts with 'w', so the walk falls off at once. Keep the word.
"rattled": walk r, a, t and land on an end mark after "rat". Stop there: replace the word with "rat".
"by": "b" is in the trie but has no child 'y', and no end mark was passed. Keep the word.
"the": no root starts with 't', so the walk falls off at once. Keep the word.
"battery": walk b, a, t and land on an end mark after "bat". Stop there: replace the word with "bat".
Result: "the cat was rat by the bat". Each word cost at most its own length, no matter how many roots there are.

recognitionSignals: For each query string, find a stored string that is a prefix of it (the shortest, the longest, or any).
Many queries against one fixed set of roots, prefixes or routes, where checking every stored string per query is too slow.
gotchas: Mark where each root ENDS; passing through a node that only continues to a longer root is not a match.
Stop at the first end mark to get the shortest root; don't keep walking for a longer one.
A word shorter than every matching path ("ab" with root "abc") is kept as it is.
confusableWith: Trie: Prefix Search asks how many stored words start with the query. This asks which stored root the query starts with: the same tree, walked for a different answer.
A hash set of roots also works: try every prefix of the word from short to long. That costs O(L²) per word for building the prefix strings, where the trie walk is O(L).

complexity.note: Here n roots and q sentence words, each at most L letters. Building the trie touches up to n · L nodes, and each word walks at most L of them before it stops. The trie holds up to n · L nodes; the new sentence is the output.
